What the model can and can’t trace

children.label: What the model can and can’t trace

children.value: follows supply chains through the 66 countries in the multi-region table. The 83 Tier 3 countries are not separate parts of that table, so supply chains can’t be traced to them one by one.
How much of a U.S. product’s supply chain is in China, Germany, or Korea?
Yes. Each of the 65 countries has its own part of the table.
How much is in Kenya or Egypt specifically?
No. Imports from all Tier 3 countries are grouped into the rest-of-world region.
Do the emissions traced to the rest of the world reflect those countries?
Not directly. The region’s input recipe and emission intensities come from Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile.
Where do a Tier 3 country’s own supply chains lead?
Only to its own economy and to its imports as a whole, which are approximated with China’s supply chains.
An industry uses the same input recipe for everything it makes, its primary product and any secondary products alike. This is what lets the market shares (
) turn industry recipes into commodity recipes.
It is the standard assumption for building commodity-by-commodity tables from Supply and Use tables, and unlike the alternative (commodity technology) it never produces negative requirements.
A secondary product takes on its producer’s recipe. Using U.S. tables after
keeps secondary products, and so this effect, small.
Within a country, every buyer of a product gets the same mix of origins. If a country imports 30% of its steel from Korea, every industry that buys imported steel gets 30% of it from Korea.
Trade data record which countries trade each product, but not which industry buys the imports.
An industry that in reality buys mostly from one origin gets the national average mix instead. Where origins differ a lot in emission intensity, this can move that industry’s factors.
The rest of the world looks like four proxy economies

The rest-of-world region stands in for every country outside the multi-region table, including all Tier 3 countries, as a source of imports. Its input recipe and emission intensities are pooled from Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile. It buys nothing from other regions, so a supply chain that reaches it stays there.
Countries outside the table have no linked IO tables of their own, and these four are the lower-income OECD economies in the table.

Imports from Tier 3 countries carry the proxy economies’ emission intensities rather than their own. Supply chains can’t be traced to individual Tier 3 countries, or onward from the rest of the world to other regions.
Data-year recipes, shares, and intensities still apply in 2024

The IO tables, emissions, trade shares, and gap-fill shares come from different years (for example, 2024 trade data with IO tables and emissions from 2018 to 2023). We assume the input recipes, origin shares, and emission intensities from each source’s data year still describe the 2024 economy. Each country’s emissions are divided by its output from the same year; that output is re-priced to 2024 dollars with a U.S. price index, so its direct emission intensities are data-year intensities per 2024 dollar.
National tables, multi-regional databases, and trade data are published on different schedules, and we use the most recent of each.

Where an economy’s structure, trading partners, or emission intensity changed between the data year and 2024 (for example, a cleaner electricity grid), the model reflects the earlier pattern.
